message.content: Although an Leshy, Pebble Spring became immediately fascinated by the mortal settlements when they set foot in a city. They loves the nicely paved ground, the intricate bridges, and the most of all, they loved houses. The nicely layed out stone walls forming shelters from the weathers yet connect the earth with the stories from every family. They decided to learn the craft of housebuilding with the help of a touch of arcane magic from their self-made staff. Pebble Spring wandered through the cobblestone streets, observing how the mortar between bricks held everything together with quiet strength. Each building told a story of its own, from the humblest cottage to the grandest tower. They pressed their mossy hands against the rough surfaces, feeling the years embedded in every crack. The old masons in the village were not particularly welcoming at first, viewing the Leshy as a curiosity. But Pebble Spring's earnest determination slowly won their trust, one conversation at a time. An elderly woman named Thessaly agreed to share her knowledge of foundation laying. She explained how the earth beneath the soil must be read carefully before any stone was placed. Pebble Spring listened intently, their leafy ears perking forward with every detail. The first attempts at building were clumsy, with stones tumbling in unexpected directions. The arcane magic in their staff helped stabilize the structures, though it sometimes caused the mortar to glow an odd purple. Neighbours would gather to watch the strange Leshy constructing a small garden shed behind the bakery. Children especially delighted in seeing Pebble Spring's branches reach around corners to place stones they could not otherwise. Weeks turned into months, and the garden shed grew into a proper three-room cottage. The masons began to visit Pebble Spring's work site, offering corrections and occasional praise. One autumn evening, Thessaly placed a small stone on the cornerstone, a gesture of full acceptance. Pebble Spring felt a warmth spread through their bark that no amount of sunlight could replicate. By winter, they had completed two additional structures for the village, each one more refined than the last. The cottages featured root-like foundations that merged seamlessly with the surrounding earth. Villagers marveled at how the buildings seemed to breathe with the seasons, expanding slightly in summer and settling in winter. The villagers often described Pebble Spring's newly constructed homes with a mixture of admiration and gentle humor, noting how the moss and lichen on the walls gave each structure its own distinctive character and spotty appearance that changed with every passing season of the year.
